title: Fidelity Estimates 2026 Retirees Will Need $185,500 for Healthcare Costs
excerpt: The 7.5% jump from last year is the sharpest increase in over a decade, driven by rising drug prices, higher Medicare premiums, and growing chronic condition costs.
body:
• Retirees in 2026 will need an average of $185,500 for healthcare costs, a 7.5% increase from 2025's estimate of $172,500.
  • The rise in healthcare costs is driven by increasing drug prices, Medicare premiums, and higher utilization of healthcare services as the population ages.
  • 54% of preretirees mistakenly believe that Medicare covers all health expenses, excluding long-term care.
  • Only 25% of Americans are currently contributing to Health Savings Accounts, which are recommended for managing healthcare costs in retirement.
Key Takeaways
  • Retirees in 2026 will need $185,500 for healthcare, a 7.5% increase from last year.
  • Rising drug prices and Medicare premiums drive the largest healthcare cost jump since 2015.
  • 54% of preretirees wrongly believe Medicare covers all health expenses, excluding long-term care.
  • Only 25% of Americans contribute to Health Savings Accounts, a recommended financial tool.

Fidelity's 25th annual estimate

Americans retiring at 65 this year face an average healthcare bill of $185,500 over their remaining lifetimes, according to Fidelity Investments' 25th annual Retiree Health Care Cost Estimate released on Tuesday. The figure marks a 7.5% increase from last year's $172,500 projection — the steepest annual jump in more than a decade.

The estimate covers Medicare premiums, out-of-pocket prescription drug costs, and medical expenses including copayments, coinsurance, and deductibles. It assumes enrollment in traditional Medicare Parts A and B, along with a Part D prescription drug plan.

What's Driving the Surge

Fidelity pointed to several converging forces behind the spike. Rising prices for care, increased healthcare utilization as Americans age, and growing costs tied to managing chronic conditions all contributed. The popularity of high-priced drugs — including GLP-1 weight-loss medications — and expensive therapies such as cell and cancer treatments have added upward pressure across the system, according to Investopedia.

Medicare premiums themselves climbed in 2026. The standard Part B premium rose to $202.90 per month, a $17.90 increase from 2025, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The annual Part B deductible increased to $283, and the Part A hospital deductible jumped to $1,736 per benefit period.

"Financial planning for retirement is about more than reaching a savings target, especially as retirement itself continues to evolve."

— Shams Talib, Head of Fidelity Workplace Consulting

The Medicare Gap Most Retirees Don't See

A striking finding from Fidelity's accompanying survey: 54% of preretirees incorrectly believe Medicare will cover all of their health expenses. In reality, Medicare involves premiums and cost-sharing, and the program leaves significant gaps.

According to Barron's, nearly 45% of Fidelity's total estimate comes from Part B and Part D premiums alone. Another 48% consists of copayments, deductibles, and coinsurance, while out-of-pocket prescription drug expenses account for the remaining 7%.

More than half of Medicare beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Advantage — the privately run alternative to traditional Medicare — where costs stack up differently. While many Advantage plans bundle drug coverage at no extra charge, they impose higher costs for out-of-network care. For 2026, the maximum allowed out-of-pocket cap is $9,250 for in-network coverage and $13,900 for combined in- and out-of-network services.

Long-Term Care: The Excluded Wild Card

Fidelity's estimate does not include long-term care expenses, which represent a separate and potentially larger financial burden. A nonmedical caregiver in the home costs more than $80,000 a year, assisted living runs a median $74,400 annually, and a private nursing home room tops $129,000 per year, according to CareScout data cited by MarketWatch.

Understanding Medicare Coverage Gaps

About 70% of adults who survive to 65 develop severe long-term care needs before they die, and 48% receive some form of paid care over their lifetime, according to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

"Medicare is a critical part of retirement health coverage, but it does not eliminate every healthcare expense."

— Steve Betts, Head of Fidelity Health

Planning Tools and HSA Strategy

Despite the daunting figures, financial planners emphasize that these costs are spread over decades, not paid in a lump sum. The primary tool experts recommend is a Health Savings Account. HSAs offer a triple tax advantage: contributions are pretax, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are also tax-free. Balances roll over annually and remain portable across employers.

Yet only 25% of Americans currently contribute to an HSA to help cover healthcare costs in retirement, Fidelity found. And among those who do, 40% keep their balance in cash rather than investing it — leaving potential growth on the table.

For Indian Americans weighing retirement in the U.S. versus returning to India, the $185,500 figure adds another data point to a complex calculation. Healthcare in India remains significantly cheaper, but access to Medicare requires U.S. residency, and the program does not cover care received abroad. Those who split time between both countries must budget for dual healthcare systems — and should factor in that Fidelity's estimate assumes continuous U.S.-based Medicare enrollment.

The annual estimate arrives as more than 11,000 Americans turn 65 each day, a pace that will continue through 2027. With healthcare costs consistently outpacing inflation, early planning remains critical.
